2	# Measuring and Analyzing GPU Kernel Performance
3	
4	GPU kernel optimization involves two separate questions: how fast the operation is, and where its
5	time goes. A benchmark answers the first question; a profile helps answer the second.
6	
7	One Python call does not necessarily correspond to one GPU kernel. It may launch several kernels,
8	enqueue memory copies, or wait for GPU work to finish. Before timing, define which of those steps
9	belong to the operation and use the same boundary for every implementation.
10	
11	The performance chapter ({ref}`chap_performance`) uses roofline analysis to reason about compute and
12	memory limits. Here the focus shifts to experiments: defining the timing boundary, choosing warm-up
13	and repeat budgets, and reading profiler reports.
14	
15	## Separate Measurement from Diagnosis
16	
17	The tools used in this workflow have different jobs:
18	
19	| Tool | Primary question |
20	|---|---|
21	| CUDA events | How much GPU-stream time elapsed across the measured region? A stream is an ordered queue of GPU work. |
22	| Synchronized wall-clock timer | How much wall-clock time elapsed between starting a host call and completing all GPU work required by it? |
23	| Proton (provided by Triton) | Which GPU kernels were launched, how often, and which kernels account for most of the time? |
24	| Nsight Systems | How do host work, streams, copies, kernels, and communication overlap on a timeline? |
25	| Nsight Compute (`ncu`) | What is the selected kernel doing internally, and which resource or stall should be investigated next? |
26	| IKET (optional) | After adding in-kernel markers, when do marked phases run, and where do warp roles wait or overlap? |
27	
28	## Verify Correctness Before Timing
29	
30	Verify correctness before measuring performance:
31	
32	1. Construct representative inputs, including relevant boundary cases.
33	2. Run the implementation and synchronize so that GPU work has completed.
34	3. Compare the output with a reference under a stated tolerance.
35	4. If the kernel accumulates into an existing output or modifies an input in place, restore the same
36	   initial state before each correctness check.
37	
38	For a custom GEMM, let `actual` be the implementation's output. One possible reference is a PyTorch
39	GEMM computed in FP32 and then converted to the target output type:
40	
41	```python
42	import torch
43	
44	
45	torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("highest")
46	actual = my_gemm(a, b)  # replace with your implementation
47	torch.cuda.synchronize()
48	expected = torch.mm(a.float(), b.float()).to(actual.dtype)
49	rtol = 1e-2  # example only; adjust for the output dtype, accumulation, and shape
50	atol = 1e-2
51	torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
52	```
53	
54	`torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("highest")` prevents PyTorch from using reduced-precision
55	internal computation for this CUDA FP32 reference. The example `rtol` and `atol` specify the relative
56	and absolute error tolerances. The value `1e-2` is only a practical starting point; adjust it for the
57	output dtype, accumulation method, shape, and operator contract. Use the same reference and
58	tolerances throughout one comparison.
59	
60	Keep the reference computation and result comparison outside the timed region. Whether state reset
61	is timed depends on the operation boundary defined in the next section.
62	
63	## Define the Timing Boundary
64	
65	Before timing, define the work that constitutes one measured operation. It may contain only one
66	kernel, or it may include every kernel, memory copy, and state reset required to produce the complete
67	result. State explicitly whether compilation, input construction, allocation, or data conversion is
68	part of that operation. Implementations are directly comparable only when they perform the same work
69	inside the measured boundary.
70	
71	The GEMM-plus-ReLU example later in this chapter can use three different boundaries. CUDA events
72	around `torch.mm` measure GEMM GPU-stream time. Events around the complete `run()` measure
73	GEMM-plus-ReLU GPU-stream time. A CPU timer started before `run()` and stopped after synchronizing
74	measures end-to-end latency for one Python call. Matrix allocation and warm-up remain outside all
75	three boundaries by default.
76	
77	Once the scope is defined, choose the timer:
78	
79	- **CUDA events** record timestamps when a GPU stream reaches two points. They can measure an
80	  interval on the device timeline around one kernel or a complete operator. Kernels, memory copies,
81	  and idle stream gaps inside that interval all count. For a multi-stream operation, work on every
82	  participating stream must be ordered after the start event and complete before the end event is
83	  recorded.
84	- A **synchronized wall-clock timer** starts before the host call and stops after all GPU work required
85	  by that call has completed. It also includes Python dispatch, CUDA launch, and the wait for GPU
86	  completion, so it is appropriate for end-to-end call latency.
87	
88	For example, if the stream reaches the start event before the host submits the next launch, that idle
89	stream time remains inside the CUDA event interval. A CUDA event interval is therefore not necessarily
90	the same as a kernel's start-to-finish execution interval in a profiler.
91	
92	## Measure GPU Time and Single-Call Latency
93	
94	### Measure GPU Stream Time with CUDA Events
95	
96	CUDA launches are normally asynchronous, so an unsynchronized CPU timer can stop before the GPU
97	finishes and mostly reflect host submission time. The
98	[PyTorch CUDA semantics documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html#asynchronous-execution)
99	describes this behavior. The following benchmark uses CUDA events to measure elapsed time on the
100	current stream.
101	
102	This runnable CUDA event benchmark allocates its matrices, runs a warm-up, measures an FP16
103	GEMM over five rounds, and reports the median round result:
104	
105	```python
106	from statistics import median
107	
108	import torch
109	
110	
111	a = torch.randn((2048, 2048), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
112	b = torch.randn((2048, 2048), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
113	c = torch.empty((2048, 2048), device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
114	
115	
116	def gemm():
117	    torch.mm(a, b, out=c)
118	
119	
120	def measure_batch_ms(fn, calls):
121	    """Return mean CUDA event time per call for one batch of back-to-back calls, in ms."""
122	    start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
123	    end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
124	
125	    start.record()
126	    for _ in range(calls):
127	        fn()
128	    end.record()
129	    end.synchronize()
130	    return start.elapsed_time(end) / calls
131	
132	
133	warmup_calls = 500
134	repeat = 100
135	rounds = 5
136	
137	for _ in range(warmup_calls):
138	    gemm()
139	torch.cuda.synchronize()
140	
141	samples_ms = [measure_batch_ms(gemm, repeat) for _ in range(rounds)]
142	
143	print(f"device: {torch.cuda.get_device_name()}")
144	print(f"calls per round: {repeat}")
145	print("round samples (ms):", [round(x, 4) for x in samples_ms])
146	print(f"median CUDA event time: {median(samples_ms):.4f} ms")
147	```
148	
149	`measure_batch_ms` records start and end events on the current CUDA stream and divides their elapsed
150	time by the number of calls. The result is the average GPU-stream time per GEMM across back-to-back
151	calls. `end.synchronize()` makes the CPU wait for that round of GPU work so that the event timing
152	result can be read.
153	
154	`warmup_calls=500` and `repeat=100` are invocation counts; `rounds=5` requests five independent
155	measurement batches. These values came from stability testing on the B200: results were still falling
156	after 50 warm-up calls but stabilized by 500, and `repeat=100` was more stable than `repeat=10`. For
157	another workload, first increase `warmup_calls` until the early rounds stop drifting; if variation
158	remains large, increase `repeat` or
159	`rounds`. If timings shift systematically as the run gets longer, inspect temperature, power, and
160	clock behavior.
161	
162	This code always reuses the same matrices, so it represents a warm-cache workload with repeated
163	inputs. Whether the accesses actually hit in cache still depends on the total amount of data revisited
164	by this computation and the hardware cache capacity.
165	
166	This book uses TVM's
167	[`tvm.tirx.bench.bench`](https://github.com/apache/tvm/blob/v0.26.0/python/tvm/tirx/bench.py)
168	to handle warm-up, repeated timing, and statistics. The supplied function only launches a prepared
169	implementation; inputs, outputs, and workspace remain outside the timed interval. Unlike the manual
170	warm-cache example, `bench` writes a 256 MiB buffer before each measured invocation to reduce reuse
171	of data left in L2 by the previous invocation, then records an independent CUDA event interval:
172	
173	```python
174	from tvm.tirx.bench import bench
175	
176	
177	# Reuse gemm from above. For a custom TIRx kernel, substitute its no-argument callable.
178	run = gemm
179	result = bench(
180	    {"gemm": run},
181	    timer="event",
182	    warmup=25,
183	    repeat=100,
184	    rounds=5,
185	    cooldown_s=1.0,
186	)
187	
188	print(result["impls"]["gemm"])           # five-round mean, in us
189	print(result["round_samples"]["gemm"])  # result from each round
190	```
191	
192	`warmup=25` and `repeat=100` are millisecond budgets. The event timer uses a short calibration run to
193	convert them into invocation counts. The reported event intervals cover only the measured calls; the
194	256 MiB write used to reduce L2 reuse occurs before each start event. `rounds=5` runs five rounds,
195	and `cooldown_s=1.0` pauses before each one. `impls` stores the five-round mean, while
196	`round_samples` stores the individual results. Adjust budgets
197	and rounds by the same stability criteria used above, and use the same settings for every
198	implementation.
199	
200	The `run_bench` entry points in TIRx-kernels also use this helper. Outside distributed mode, omitting
201	`timer` selects Proton by default; specify `timer="event"` for a CUDA event interval. A repeatedly
202	invoked in-place kernel must still follow the reset rule above. If reset occurs inside the measured
203	function, its cost belongs to the operation.
204	
205	### Measure End-to-End Time for One Call
206	
207	Use a synchronized wall-clock timer to measure the interval from the start of a Python call until its
208	GPU work finishes. The following code continues with the `gemm()` defined and warmed up above:
209	
210	```python
211	from statistics import median
212	import time
213	
214	import torch
215	
216	
217	def measure_single_call_ms(fn, samples=20):
218	    values = []
219	    for _ in range(samples):
220	        torch.cuda.synchronize()  # exclude unfinished work from earlier calls
221	        t0 = time.perf_counter()
222	        fn()
223	        torch.cuda.synchronize()  # wait for this call's GPU work
224	        values.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1e3)
225	    return values
226	
227	
228	host_samples_ms = measure_single_call_ms(gemm)
229	print("single-call samples (ms):", [round(x, 4) for x in host_samples_ms])
230	print(f"median end-to-end time: {median(host_samples_ms):.4f} ms")
231	```
232	
233	The first synchronization keeps unfinished earlier work outside the measurement. The second ensures
234	that this GEMM finishes before the timer stops. Each sample contains exactly one call, so the result
235	includes the Python call, CUDA launch, GPU execution, and the wait for completion. By comparison, the
236	CUDA event benchmark above reports average GPU-stream time per GEMM across back-to-back calls.
237	
238	Every implementation in a comparison must use the same timer and boundary. If both results are
239	reported, name them separately as *CUDA event GPU time* and *single-call end-to-end time* so that
240	their different boundaries remain visible.
241	
242	### Advanced: Timing a Multi-Stream Operation
243	
244	When one operation submits work to several CUDA streams, the event dependencies must ensure that
245	every branch starts after the start event and finishes before the end event is recorded. In this
246	example, `sin` and `cos` run on separate streams. The timing stream waits for both branches before
247	adding their results:
248	
249	```python
250	import torch
251	
252	
253	x = torch.randn(1 << 20, device="cuda")
254	left = torch.empty_like(x)
255	right = torch.empty_like(x)
256	output = torch.empty_like(x)
257	
258	stream_left = torch.cuda.Stream()
259	stream_right = torch.cuda.Stream()
260	timing_stream = torch.cuda.current_stream()
261	
262	start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
263	left_done = torch.cuda.Event()
264	right_done = torch.cuda.Event()
265	end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
266	
267	
268	def measure_operation_ms():
269	    torch.cuda.synchronize()
270	    start.record(timing_stream)
271	
272	    stream_left.wait_event(start)
273	    with torch.cuda.stream(stream_left):
274	        torch.sin(x, out=left)
275	    left_done.record(stream_left)
276	
277	    stream_right.wait_event(start)
278	    with torch.cuda.stream(stream_right):
279	        torch.cos(x, out=right)
280	    right_done.record(stream_right)
281	
282	    timing_stream.wait_event(left_done)
283	    timing_stream.wait_event(right_done)
284	    torch.add(left, right, out=output)
285	
286	    end.record(timing_stream)
287	    end.synchronize()
288	    return start.elapsed_time(end)
289	
290	
291	elapsed_ms = measure_operation_ms()
292	torch.testing.assert_close(output, torch.sin(x) + torch.cos(x))
293	print(f"multi-stream operation: {elapsed_ms:.4f} ms")
294	```
295	
296	`start` is the common starting signal. `left_done` and `right_done` mark the ends of the two
297	branches. The timing stream waits for both completion events, performs the final addition, and then
298	records `end`. Each `wait_event` creates a GPU-side dependency while the CPU continues submitting
299	work; only `end.synchronize()` waits on the CPU.
300	
301	The event graph is:
302	
303	```text
304	timing stream: start ──────────── wait(left_done, right_done) ─ add ─ end
305	left stream:          wait(start) ─ sin ─ left_done
306	right stream:         wait(start) ─ cos ─ right_done
307	```
308	
309	This dependency structure allows the two branches to execute concurrently; actual overlap depends on
310	their GPU resource usage. Confirm the actual execution schedule in a Nsight Systems timeline. For
311	reported measurements, call `measure_operation_ms()` several times for warm-up, then call it
312	repeatedly to collect single-call samples and report their median and variation.
313	
314	#### PDL Within One Stream
315	
316	Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL) is available to custom CUDA and DSL launch paths that explicitly
317	enable it. The primary and secondary kernels are submitted to the same stream. After the primary
318	emits a trigger, the secondary may begin preparation that does not depend on the primary's result.
319	Before consuming that result, the secondary waits on the PDL dependency.
320	
321	```text
322	primary:   initial work ─ trigger ─ remaining work
323	secondary:                    preamble ─ wait ─ dependent work
324	```
325	
326	Record `start` before launching the primary and `end` after launching the secondary. The resulting
327	CUDA event interval measures GPU-stream elapsed time for the complete launch sequence. The two
328	kernels may overlap, so the sum of their profiler durations can exceed the complete operation
329	latency. Use a Nsight Systems timeline to confirm the observed overlap.
330	
331	PDL creates an opportunity for concurrent execution, while the runtime may still serialize the
332	kernels. Validate correctness both when the kernels overlap and when the runtime serializes them. The
333	`torch.cuda.Stream` interface above does not expose PDL launch attributes; a custom CUDA or DSL
334	implementation supplies them. See the
335	[CUDA Programming Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/programmatic-dependent-launch.html)
336	for the enablement details.
337	
338	## Keep Benchmark Conditions Consistent
339	
340	The examples above measure repeated calls after allocation and warm-up. If first-call latency or a
341	complete application path is the target, include the relevant CUDA initialization, JIT compilation,
342	and autotuning in the timing boundary and report that result separately.
343	
344	Keep every per-round result and state whether the summary is a median or mean. If results continue to
345	trend across rounds, check warm-up, temperature, and clock state before summarizing the full set of
346	measurements. When comparing implementations, alternate their measurement order so that no
347	implementation is consistently measured on a colder or hotter device.
348	
349	Use one cache policy throughout the comparison. The manual example repeatedly reuses the same
350	matrices and therefore models a warm-cache workload, although the actual hit rate still depends
351	on the total amount of data revisited and the cache capacity. The TVM 0.26 CUDA event and Proton timers
352	instead write a 256 MiB buffer before each measured invocation to reduce L2 reuse; this write is
353	outside the timed interval. Choose the policy that represents the target application.
354	`torch.cuda.empty_cache()` only releases unused blocks from PyTorch's allocator; GPU L2 contents
355	remain managed by the hardware cache policy.
356	
357	Also align the following conditions across implementations:
358	
359	- **Numerical semantics:** input and output dtype, layout, transpose convention, alignment,
360	  accumulation precision, scale, mask, epilogue, output definition, and accuracy tolerance;
361	- **Measured scope:** inclusion or exclusion of allocation, conversion, state reset, auxiliary
362	  kernels, communication, and synchronization;
363	- **Tuning conditions:** workspace limits, whether per-shape autotuning is allowed, and the search
364	  budget available to each implementation.
365	
366	Record the GPU, driver, CUDA, framework, and compiler versions, along with dtype, shape, clock, and
367	power settings. For a library baseline, also record the library version, selected algorithm, and
368	workspace. Autotuning may run outside the timed interval, but its search budget and final
369	configuration are still part of the experimental setup.
370	
371	## Convert Latency to Throughput
372	
373	Compute throughput by dividing a clearly defined amount of work by the measured latency. For a
374	multiplication of an $M\times K$ matrix by a $K\times N$ matrix with latency `t_us` in
375	microseconds:
376	
377	```text
378	TFLOP/s = 2 × M × N × K / t_us / 10^6
379	```
380	
381	The numerator and timing boundary must describe the same work. The complete GEMM-plus-ReLU operation
382	below takes 105.152 μs. Dividing $2\times4096^3$ by that duration gives about 1307 TFLOP/s, but this
383	is only *effective throughput*: GEMM work divided by the complete operation time. The denominator is
384	the full operation time and therefore includes ReLU. To report the GEMM kernel's own TFLOP/s, the
385	timed interval must cover only GEMM.
386	
387	A table that reports TFLOP/s, GB/s, or tokens/s should include the underlying latency measurement and
388	explain how the work was counted. For attention and fused kernels, also state whether the numerator
389	represents the full dense problem, the elements actually selected, or the work executed by the
390	kernel. See {ref}`chap_performance` for the corresponding formulas and roofline analysis.
391	
392	## Find the Most Expensive Kernel with Proton
393	
394	From this point onward, the baseline, Proton, Nsight Systems, and Nsight Compute all run the same
395	operation from `appendix/nsys_example.py`: multiply two $4096\times4096$ BF16 matrices and then apply
396	ReLU to the result. The inputs, intermediate result, and output are allocated before timing or
397	collection. The operation in the script is:
398	
399	```python
400	def run():
401	    with torch.cuda.nvtx.range("BF16 GEMM"):
402	        torch.mm(a, b, out=c)
403	    with torch.cuda.nvtx.range("ReLU"):
404	        torch.clamp_min(c, 0, out=output)
405	```
406	
407	Before any timed or profiled run, the script runs one operation and synchronizes. It then computes an
408	FP32 `torch.mm` reference, applies ReLU, converts the result to BF16, and compares it
409	with the output using `rtol=2e-2` and `atol=1e-2`. A mismatch stops the command before the benchmark
410	or profiler begins. This preflight check is outside both the baseline timing interval and the
411	collection range used below.
412

490	## Analyze an Application Timeline with Nsight Systems
491	
492	Proton provides an aggregate ranking, but it does not show kernel ordering, gaps, copies, or host
493	waits. Nsight Systems answers those questions with a timeline.
494	
495	### Capture a Timeline for the Target Operation
496	
497	The script's `--profile-once` mode runs the warm-up while the profiler is still inactive and waits
498	for that work to finish. It then submits exactly one GEMM-plus-ReLU operation between
499	`cudaProfilerStart()` and `cudaProfilerStop()`:
500	
501	```python
502	def run_once_for_profiler(run, *, warmup_calls):
503	    for _ in range(warmup_calls):
504	        run()
505	    torch.cuda.synchronize()
506	
507	    cudart = torch.cuda.cudart()
508	    cudart.cudaProfilerStart()
509	    with torch.cuda.nvtx.range("target operation"):
510	        run()
511	        torch.cuda.synchronize()
512	    cudart.cudaProfilerStop()
513	```
514	
515	The NVTX range makes the target operation easy to locate in the timeline. Synchronization inside the
516	range ensures that both kernels finish before collection stops. `cudaProfilerStart()` and
517	`cudaProfilerStop()` only delimit the collection range; they do not measure time.
518	
519	The following command runs the script and writes `reports/target-timeline.nsys-rep`:
520	
521	```bash
522	mkdir -p reports
523	nsys profile \
524	  --trace=cuda,nvtx \
525	  --sample=none \
526	  --cpuctxsw=none \
527	  --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi \
528	  --capture-range-end=stop \
529	  --output=reports/target-timeline \
530	  --force-overwrite=true \
531	  python appendix/nsys_example.py \
532	    --size 4096 \
533	    --warmup-calls 500 \
534	    --profile-once
535	```
536	
537	`--capture-range=cudaProfilerApi` restricts collection to the interval between
538	`cudaProfilerStart()` and `cudaProfilerStop()`. `--trace=cuda,nvtx` records CUDA APIs, GPU activity,
539	and NVTX ranges. CPU sampling and context-switch tracing are disabled here to keep the report focused
540	on the CUDA timeline. If that timeline contains a long GPU gap, collect a separate report with the
541	relevant host-scheduling or OS runtime tracing enabled.
542	
543	Once the report has been generated, open its timeline in the Nsight Systems GUI:
544	
545	```bash
546	nsys-ui reports/target-timeline.nsys-rep
547	```

629	## Use Nsight Compute to Analyze a Single Kernel
630	
631	Use Nsight Systems to select the target kernel and NCU to explain its hardware behavior. This section
632	begins with a reusable workflow, applies it to a BF16 GEMM on a B200, and then explains the supporting
633	metrics and calculations.
634	
635	### How to Read an NCU Report
636	
637	An SM (streaming multiprocessor) is a GPU compute unit that hosts thread blocks and executes their
638	instructions. A warp contains 32 threads and is the basic group that a scheduler selects when issuing
639	an instruction. A block or warp is resident from the time it is assigned to an SM until it finishes.
640	
641	Analyze a new NCU report in this order:
642	
643	| Current question | Where to look first | Purpose |
644	|---|---|---|
645	| Which kernel does this report describe? | Kernel, device, and grid/block in the report header, plus Warnings/Errors | Confirm the filter and collection result |
646	| Does the launch expose enough device-wide parallelism? | `Grid Size` and `Waves Per SM` in `LaunchStats` | Determine whether the grid provides enough device-wide parallelism |
647	| How much work can reside on each SM at once? | `Block Limit` fields and theoretical/achieved occupancy in `Occupancy` | Quantify theoretical and achieved residency, and identify which resources set the theoretical limit |
648	| Which part of the hardware should be investigated first? | Compute, Memory, and DRAM throughput in `SpeedOfLight` | Choose the compute, memory, or scheduling path |
649	| Can the scheduler consistently find an instruction to issue? | `Scheduler Statistics` → `Warps Per Scheduler`; when few warps are ready to issue an instruction, continue to `Warp State Statistics` → `Warp State (All Cycles)` | Compare resident, ready, and issued warps; inspect the main wait states when ready work is scarce |
650	
651	`Grid Size` is the number of blocks submitted by the launch. `Waves Per SM` is the grid size divided
652	by the number of blocks that could theoretically reside across the whole GPU at once. A value of 1
653	means the two counts are equal; 3.46 means that the grid contains 3.46 times the device-wide theoretical
654	resident-block capacity. This ratio helps determine whether the grid contains enough blocks to cover
655	the GPU. It does not record the actual block-scheduling order.
656	
657	Each `Block Limit` reports how many blocks one SM could host if registers, shared memory, threads, or
658	another listed resource were the only constraint. The smallest value sets the theoretical block
659	limit. Theoretical occupancy is the maximum resident-warp count allowed by those limits, expressed as
660	a fraction of the hardware capacity. Achieved occupancy is the average active-warp count observed
661	during collection, expressed as a fraction of the same capacity. These metrics describe resident
662	concurrency; scheduler metrics show whether that concurrency affects instruction issue.
663	
664	In `SpeedOfLight`, Compute represents the busiest SM compute path, while Memory represents the
665	busiest memory-side path. DRAM specifically measures the external-memory interface. Each uses its own
666	sustainable peak as the denominator. On a B200, HBM provides external device memory, L2 is shared
667	across the GPU, and L1TEX is the SM-side path that handles memory requests. A high Memory value means
668	that some memory-side path is busy; DRAM shows whether the external HBM interface is near saturation.
669	In `ComputeWorkloadAnalysis`, active cycles show when a pipeline still has work in flight, while
670	`Issue Slots Busy` reports how many scheduler issue opportunities were used.
671	
672	`SchedulerStats` distinguishes several warp states. An active warp is resident and unfinished. An
673	eligible warp has a decoded next instruction whose dependencies are ready and whose required
674	execution unit is available. An issued warp has issued an instruction in the current cycle.
675	After confirming the target launch and examining the grid, residency, and `SpeedOfLight`, select the
676	next metrics:
677	
678	- **Compute is closer to its peak:** In `ComputeWorkloadAnalysis`, open
679	  `Pipe Utilization (Elapsed Cycles)` → `Pipe Utilization (% of elapsed cycles)` and find the compute
680	  path with the most active cycles. Then inspect `Issue Slots Busy` in the same section's summary.
681	  If one path keeps processing work while most issue slots remain empty, continue to
682	  `Scheduler Statistics` → `Warps Per Scheduler` to explain the low instruction-issue rate.
683	- **Memory is closer to its peak:** Collect `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis`,
684	  `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis_Chart`, and `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis_Tables`. First follow the data path
685	  through DRAM, L2, and L1/TEX under `Memory Workload Analysis Chart` → `Memory Chart`. Then read
686	  throughput, read/write bytes, hit rate, and the shared- and local-memory fields under
687	  `Memory Workload Analysis Tables` → `Memory Tables`. If DRAM is also near its peak, investigate
688	  external HBM traffic first. If DRAM is low, shift attention to L2, L1/TEX, shared memory, or local
689	  memory. Local memory is a per-thread private address space; its physical traffic traverses the
690	  L1/L2 caches and external device memory.
691	- **Compute and Memory are both low:** Use the grid size and waves to determine whether the launch
692	  provides enough blocks to cover the GPU. If it does not, inspect the grid, block, and cluster
693	  configuration or divide the work into more blocks. If it does, inspect `SchedulerStats`. If active
694	  warps exist but eligible warps are scarce, use `WarpStateStats` to see whether they are waiting on
695	  data, synchronization, or another dependency.
696	- **Compute and Memory are both high:** Expand both sides, identify one specific bottleneck candidate
697	  on each side, and change one factor at a time to determine which candidate affects kernel time.
698	
699	`MemoryWorkloadAnalysis` summarizes traffic and cache behavior for the whole kernel across DRAM, L2,
700	L1TEX, and other memory paths. `SourceCounters` then maps sampled stalls and instruction activity to
701	SASS (GPU machine instructions) or source locations to help trace a specific load dependency.
702	
703	Interpret “high” and “low” in the context of the current GPU and workload, and compare values from the
704	same report. Once the evidence points to a specific code change and supports a prediction about how
705	the relevant metrics and latency should respond, the current pass has produced a testable hypothesis.
706	If the scope is still too broad, collect the next section along the relevant path above.
707	
708	### Worked Example: A B200 BF16 GEMM
709	
710	#### 1. Collect the First `basic` Report
711	
712	Continue using the script's `--profile-once` mode. The application submits one GEMM and then one ReLU
713	inside the collection range; NCU waits for the range to begin and profiles only the GEMM:
714	
715	```bash
716	mkdir -p reports
717	ncu \
718	  --config-file off \
719	  --profile-from-start off \
720	  --kernel-name 'regex:.*nvjet_sm100.*' \
721	  --launch-count 1 \
722	  --set basic \
723	  --replay-mode kernel \
724	  --cache-control all \
725	  --clock-control boost \
726	  --pipeline-boost-state stable \
727	  --export reports/bf16-gemm-basic \
728	  --force-overwrite \
729	  python appendix/nsys_example.py \
730	    --size 4096 \
731	    --warmup-calls 500 \
732	    --profile-once
733	```
734	
735	The key options control the capture range, target, metrics, and collection conditions:
736	
737	- `--profile-from-start off` makes NCU wait until the script calls `cudaProfilerStart()`.
738	- `--kernel-name` selects kernels in that range whose names contain `nvjet_sm100`, and
739	  `--launch-count 1` produces a report for the first matching launch. The expression comes from the
740	  preceding timeline; replace it with the name from your own program.
741	- `--set basic` collects the launch, occupancy, and high-level throughput sections needed for this
742	  first pass.
743	- `--replay-mode kernel` allows NCU to replay the selected GEMM while collecting hardware counters.
744	  `--cache-control all` flushes controllable caches before replay, while the remaining options control
745	  clocks and pipeline boost state during collection. Kernel replay is appropriate here because this
746	  GEMM can be replayed independently. Workloads with cross-kernel dependencies or concurrency need a
747	  replay mode that preserves the required application or range state.
748	
749	Here, “one GEMM” means one launch submitted by the application. NCU can still replay that GEMM
750	internally to collect all requested hardware counters. The 500 warm-up calls stay outside the
751	collection range, avoiding initialization and lazy-loading work. NCU's cache control then changes the
752	normal warm-cache conditions.
753	
754	Open the report in the GUI:
755	
756	```bash
757	ncu-ui reports/bf16-gemm-basic.ncu-rep
758	```
759	
760	Without a GUI, print the Details page in the terminal:
761	
762	```bash
763	ncu --import reports/bf16-gemm-basic.ncu-rep \
764	    --page details \
765	    --print-details all \
766	    --print-metric-name label-name
767	```
768	
769	See the [Nsight Compute CLI documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/NsightComputeCli/)
770	for other filters and collection options. If NCU reports `ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM`, follow NVIDIA's
771	[counter-permission guidance](https://developer.nvidia.com/nvidia-development-tools-solutions-err-nvgpuctrperm-nsightcompute)
772	or ask the system administrator to enable access.
773	
774	#### 2. Use the `basic` Report to Choose What to Investigate
775	
776	First confirm the device, kernel name, grid and block dimensions, and warnings in the report header.
777	Once they match the intended launch, use these three observations to choose what to inspect next:
778	
779	| Observation in `basic` | Next step in this example |
780	|---|---|
781	| `Grid Size = 512 blocks`; `Waves Per SM = 3.46` | The grid supplies enough blocks to cover all SMs; next check how much work can reside on each SM |
782	| The register and shared-memory `Block Limit` values are both 1; theoretical/achieved occupancy is 12.50%/8.97% | Each SM can theoretically host at most eight resident warps, while the observed average is lower; use scheduler metrics to inspect instruction readiness |
783	| Compute 77.74%, Memory 38.71%, DRAM 12.88% | Compute is closest to its own peak, so expand the compute side first; aggregate HBM throughput across the device still has ample headroom |
784	
785	Start with `Waves Per SM`. The current resource limits allow one resident block per SM, and this B200
786	has 148 SMs, so the theoretical device-wide residency capacity is 148 blocks. The grid contains 512
787	blocks, and $512 / 148 = 3.46$: its block count is 3.46 times that theoretical capacity.
788	This calculation only explains the capacity ratio reported by NCU. Because this example uses
789	thread-block clusters, use the reported `Waves Per SM = 3.46` as the authoritative value. The ratio
790	confirms that the grid contains enough blocks to cover the device.
791	
792	Next consider occupancy. A B200 SM can hold at most 2,048 threads. At 32 threads per warp, that is a
793	hardware limit of 64 warps. This launch configuration permits at most one 256-thread block per SM, or
794	eight resident warps, so its theoretical occupancy is $8 / 64 = 12.50\%$. The launch can therefore
795	use at most 12.50% of the hardware's warp-residency capacity. `Achieved Occupancy = 8.97%` is the
796	observed average active-warp count expressed as a fraction of that same capacity, below the 12.50%
797	theoretical maximum. The theoretical value establishes that all schedulers on one SM
798	have at most eight resident warps in total; `SchedulerStats` then reports how many warps assigned to
799	each scheduler are ready on average.
800	
801	Finally, compare throughput. Compute is closer to its peak than Memory, so investigate the compute
802	side first. The term `compute-bound` makes a stronger claim: further speedup is ultimately constrained
803	by the throughput limit of the compute units. The `basic` report only identifies where to begin the
804	investigation. The follow-up report shows that issue opportunities are rarely used and most scheduler
805	cycles have no eligible (ready) warp; calling the kernel `compute-bound` at this point would hide that
806	key clue.
807	
808	The grid is large enough to cover the whole device, but each SM can host at most eight resident
809	warps, and the compute side is closest to its peak. The next report expands the compute pipelines and
810	collects scheduler metrics.
811	
812	#### 3. Collect Follow-Up Metrics Along the Compute Path
813	
814	The next command collects all three sections in a single run. Read them in the order
815	`ComputeWorkloadAnalysis` → `SchedulerStats` → `WarpStateStats`. For a new kernel, decide whether to
816	add each section after reading the preceding one.
817	
818	```bash
819	ncu \
820	  --config-file off \
821	  --profile-from-start off \
822	  --kernel-name 'regex:.*nvjet_sm100.*' \
823	  --launch-count 1 \
824	  --section ComputeWorkloadAnalysis \
825	  --section SchedulerStats \
826	  --section WarpStateStats \
827	  --replay-mode kernel \
828	  --cache-control all \
829	  --clock-control boost \
830	  --pipeline-boost-state stable \
831	  --export reports/bf16-gemm-followup \
832	  --force-overwrite \
833	  python appendix/nsys_example.py \
834	    --size 4096 \
835	    --warmup-calls 500 \
836	    --profile-once
837	```
838	
839	This is an independent NCU run. Percentages can vary slightly between the reports—for example,
840	77.74% becomes 78.39%—without indicating a performance change. The earlier `basic` report selected
841	the investigation path; the follow-up report uses compute, scheduler, and warp-state metrics from
842	one collection to narrow the investigation.
843	
844	#### 4. Read the Three Sections in Order
845	
846	Start with `ComputeWorkloadAnalysis` → `Pipe Utilization (Elapsed Cycles)` →
847	`Pipe Utilization (% of elapsed cycles)`. This is the active-cycle view. `Tensor (FP)` is the
848	floating-point tensor-compute path. `TMEM (Tensor Memory)` is an on-chip memory path that serves
849	tensor operations; it is distinct from external HBM/DRAM and from TMA, the asynchronous data-movement
850	engine. These paths are active for about 78% of clock cycles, while the same section's summary reports
851	`Issue Slots Busy = 3.20%`. A multi-cycle operation can issue once and keep a pipeline active, so
852	high active-cycle utilization can coexist with a low instruction issue rate.
853	
854	Next, open `Scheduler Statistics` → `Warps Per Scheduler` to see why the scheduler issues new
855	instructions so infrequently. Each scheduler has an average of 1.44 active warps that have not
856	finished, but only 0.04 eligible (ready) warps; 0.04 is an average warp count, not 4%. The denominator
857	for `No Eligible` includes only cycles in which the scheduler's SM subpartition has at least one warp
858	in flight. A value of 96.11% means that no eligible warp is available in 96.11% of those cycles. This
859	explains the low 3.20% issue rate. The SM has resident work, but most of the time no warp is ready to
860	continue.
861	
862	Finally, open `Warp State Statistics` → `Warp State (All Cycles)` to see what those warps are waiting
863	for. One warp spending one clock cycle in a state contributes one warp-cycle. Each issued warp
864	instruction corresponds to 37.00 warp-cycles, of which 32.11—about 87%—are attributed to
865	`Long Scoreboard`. This 87% is the share of warp-state cycles after normalization by issued warp
866	instructions, not a share of kernel execution time. A scoreboard is the hardware
867	dependency table that records whether results of earlier operations are ready. `Long Scoreboard`
868	means that the next instruction is still waiting for a memory operation handled by L1TEX. L1TEX is
869	the SM-side path for global, local, surface, and texture memory requests; the requested data may
870	ultimately come from L1, L2, or DRAM, so this field alone cannot identify which memory level served
871	the request. `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis` characterizes aggregate L1, L2, and DRAM behavior for the whole
872	kernel; use the SASS/source view in `SourceCounters` to narrow the investigation to specific load
873	instructions.
874	
875	Together, the three sections tell this story:
876	
877	```text
878	Tensor/TMEM paths are often active
879	→ the scheduler issues few new instructions
880	→ most cycles have no eligible (ready) warp
881	→ Long Scoreboard is the largest wait category
882	```
883	
884	Start with the L1TEX-related data dependency. Each SM can host at most eight resident warps, leaving
885	fewer independent warps available to run while another warp waits for data. In the earlier `basic`
886	report, `DRAM Throughput = 12.88%` shows that aggregate HBM bandwidth is far from saturation; individual
887	requests can still reach DRAM and incur long latency. Investigate the data dependency first, then see
888	whether Tensor Core throughput becomes the next limit. The `nvjet` GEMM in this example is a library
889	implementation, so the next report can collect `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis` and compare aggregate L1,
890	L2, and DRAM traffic, throughput, and cache behavior for the whole kernel.
891	
892	For a kernel you control, the report suggests two directions that can be tested separately:
893	
894	- **Increase resident warps:** Adjust the tile, block, or resource usage so that more work can reside
895	  on each SM.
896	- **Shorten the data-dependency wait:** Hold residency constant and move the load or prefetch
897	  earlier, or shorten the dependency chain.
898	
899	The later section “Test the Hypothesis with a Code Change” gives the concrete modifications and
900	validation steps.
901	
902	### Metric Calculations, Units, and Boundaries
903	
904	The main walkthrough already established the reading order and the conclusion for this kernel. The
905	following sections serve as a reference for complete field lists, calculations, units, and boundaries
906	that are easy to misread; consult them as needed for another kernel.
907	
908	#### `LaunchStats` and `Occupancy`
909	
910	The `LaunchStats` fields used in this example are:
911	
912	| Field | Value in this report |
913	|---|---:|
914	| `Grid Size` | 512 blocks |
915	| `Block Size` | 256 threads |
916	| `Cluster Size` | 4 blocks |
917	| `Waves Per SM` | 3.46 |
918	
919	- `Block Size = 256` means that each block has 256 threads, or eight warps. This value enters the
920	  occupancy calculation below.
921	- `Cluster Size = 4` groups every four blocks into one thread-block cluster, giving 128 clusters in
922	  the grid. The cluster's blocks are scheduled together according to a layout supported by the
923	  hardware.
924	- For cluster launches, including this one, use the `Waves Per SM` value reported by NCU; use
925	  `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters` to calculate resident clusters programmatically.
926	
927	Per-block resource usage appears in `LaunchStats`:
928	
929	| Field | Value in this report |
930	|---|---:|
931	| `Registers Per Thread` | 255 |
932	| `Dynamic Shared Memory Per Block` | 213.28 KB |
933	
934	The `Occupancy` section shows the residency permitted by those resources:
935	
936	| Field | Value in this report |
937	|---|---:|
938	| `Block Limit Registers` | 1 block / SM |
939	| `Block Limit Shared Mem` | 1 block / SM |
940	| `Theoretical Occupancy` | 12.50% |
941	| `Achieved Occupancy` | 8.97% |
942	
943	When a block becomes resident, the SM reserves its registers and shared memory. The
944	[NVIDIA Blackwell Tuning Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/blackwell-tuning-guide/index.html#occupancy)
945	specifies 65,536 32-bit registers, 228 KB of shared memory, and at most 2,048 resident threads per
946	B200 SM.
947	
948	- `Registers Per Thread = 255`. With 256 threads, one block needs about
949	  $255 \times 256 = 65{,}280$ registers, nearly the entire register file. Two blocks would need
950	  130,560 registers, exceeding 65,536.
951	- `Dynamic Shared Memory Per Block = 213.28 KB`. One block already uses most of the 228 KB available;
952	  two blocks would need at least 426.56 KB and cannot reside together.
953	- `Block Limit Registers = 1` and `Block Limit Shared Mem = 1` are the result of those two resource
954	  calculations. Either resource alone permits only one resident block per SM. NCU's exact calculation
955	  also accounts for allocation granularity and driver-reserved shared memory.
956	- `Achieved Occupancy = 8.97%` is the average active-warp ratio observed during collection, not
957	  “percent of peak kernel performance.” It is below 12.50%, so execution did not sustain the
958	  theoretical residency limit throughout the launch. The two percentages measure residency, not
959	  closeness to peak performance.
960	
961	#### `SpeedOfLight` Denominators and `Duration`
962	
963	The `SpeedOfLight` section reports these four fields:
964	
965	| Field | Value in this report |
966	|---|---:|
967	| `Duration` | 95.30 μs |
968	| `Compute (SM) Throughput` | 77.74% |
969	| `Memory Throughput` | 38.71% |
970	| `DRAM Throughput` | 12.88% |
971	
972	Interpret `Duration` only within the profiling run that produced it. This NCU capture reports
973	95.30 μs, while a separate Nsight Systems capture reports 92.608 μs. Compare implementations with the
974	unprofiled CUDA event baseline. NCU also controls clocks, flushes caches, and may replay or serialize
975	kernels; see
976	[Nsight Compute's workload-duration guidance](https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#workload-durations).
977	
978	The three throughput percentages use separate hardware peaks as their denominators. They cannot be
979	added and do not represent fractions of execution time. The
980	[Nsight Compute Profiling Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html#metrics-structure)
981	defines throughput metrics and their constituents.
982	
983	#### Compute Pipelines, the Scheduler, and Warp States
984	
985	##### `Compute Throughput Breakdown` Fields
986	
987	The report location is `SpeedOfLight` → `GPU Throughput Breakdown` →
988	`Compute Throughput Breakdown`:
989	
990	| Field | Value in this report |
991	|---|---:|
992	| `SM: Mem Tensor Cycles Active` | 77.74% |
993	| `SM: Pipe Tc Cycles Active` | 77.48% |
994	| `SM: Pipe Tensor Cycles Active` | 77.42% |
995	| `SM: Pipe Alu Cycles Active` | 1.36% |
996	| `SM: Pipe Tma Cycles Active` | 1.10% |
997	| `SM: Pipe Fma Cycles Active` | 0.61% |
998	
999	- `Mem Tensor` is an on-chip path related to Blackwell tensor memory. External data is stored in
1000	  DRAM/HBM, while TMA handles asynchronous multidimensional transfers; these three names refer to
1001	  distinct hardware paths. At 77.74%, `Mem Tensor` is the most heavily utilized compute-side path in
1002	  this report.
1003	- `Pipe Tc` and `Pipe Tensor` are two distinct pipeline counters in NCU. Both are near 77%,
1004	  consistent with a BF16 GEMM performing substantial tensor-core MMA work. They may cover
1005	  overlapping hardware activity, so read them separately; summing them would double-count activity.
1006	- `Pipe Alu` primarily corresponds to general integer and logic operations, while `Pipe Fma` covers
1007	  ordinary FP32 arithmetic and some integer multiply-add operations. At 1.36% and 0.61%, respectively,
1008	  this GEMM does not approach the peak of either path.
1009	- `Pipe Tma` corresponds to Tensor Memory Accelerator's asynchronous data-movement path. Its 1.10%
1010	  value shows that TMA is far from its own peak. Data supply also involves TMEM, caches, shared
1011	  memory, and dependency latency, each described by other metrics.
1012	
1013	##### The Two `Pipe Utilization` Denominators
1014	
1015	The `ComputeWorkloadAnalysis` summary reports `Issue Slots Busy = 3.20%`. The report labels the two
1016	views `Pipe Utilization (% of elapsed cycles)` and
1017	`Pipe Utilization (% of peak instructions executed over elapsed cycles)`.
1018	
1019	Putting each pipeline on one row makes the contrast easier to see:
1020	
1021	| Pipeline field | Active-cycle view | Instruction-rate view |
1022	|---|---:|---:|
1023	| `TMEM (Tensor Memory)` | 78.39% | 0.04% |
1024	| `TC` | 78.12% | 0.38% |
1025	| `Tensor (FP)` | 78.07% | 0.61% |
1026	
1027	The two views use different denominators: one reports active pipeline cycles, while the other reports
1028	instruction execution rate relative to peak. Their values cannot be added or subtracted.
1029	
1030	##### Complete `SchedulerStats` Fields
1031	
1032	The report location is `Scheduler Statistics` → `Warps Per Scheduler`:
1033	
1034	| Field | Value in this report |
1035	|---|---:|
1036	| `GPU Maximum Warps Per Scheduler` | 16 |
1037	| `Theoretical Warps Per Scheduler` | 2.00 |
1038	| `Active Warps Per Scheduler` | 1.44 |
1039	| `Eligible Warps Per Scheduler` | 0.04 |
1040	| `Issued Warp Per Scheduler` | 0.04 |
1041	
1042	The summary in the same section also reports `No Eligible = 96.11%`.
1043	
1044	`GPU Maximum = 16` is the hardware capacity of one scheduler. `Theoretical = 2.00` comes from this
1045	kernel's theoretical maximum of eight resident warps per SM divided among four schedulers.
1046	
1047	##### `WarpStateStats` Normalization
1048	
1049	One warp spending one cycle in a state contributes one warp-cycle; four warps spending the same cycle
1050	in a state contribute four warp-cycles. NCU then normalizes those cycles by the number of issued warp
1051	instructions. The report summary gives the first field below, and `Warp State (All Cycles)` gives the
1052	second:
1053	
1054	| Field | Value in this report |
1055	|---|---:|
1056	| `Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction` | 37.00 warp-cycles / issued instruction |
1057	| `Stall Long Scoreboard` | 32.11 warp-cycles / issued instruction |
1058	
1059	The report shows an average of 37.00 warp-cycles per issued warp instruction. Of those, 32.11, or
1060	about 86.8%, are assigned to `Long Scoreboard`. These values are normalized across all warps and use
1061	warp-cycles / issued instruction, a different unit from the scheduler's average issue rate.
1062	
1063	The `Est. Speedup` shown next to an NCU rule is a model-based estimate of the potential reduction in
1064	workload time for that rule. Use it to prioritize the investigation; only a benchmark of the modified
1065	kernel can establish the actual speedup.
1066	
1067	##### Other Common Warp States
1068	
1069	| Warp state | Direct meaning | What to inspect next |
1070	|---|---|---|
1071	| `Short Scoreboard` | Usually waiting for shared memory or another on-chip unit to produce a result | Inspect shared-memory accesses and the corresponding source |
1072	| `Barrier` | Waiting for other warps to reach a synchronization point | Compare the work assigned to different warps and when they arrive |
1073	| `Not Selected` | The warp is ready, but another warp was selected in this cycle | Check whether many ready warps are competing for issue opportunities |
1074	
1075	#### Correlate Metrics with SASS and Source Code Using `SourceCounters`
1076	
1077	`WarpStateStats` summarizes wait states across the entire kernel. `SourceCounters` narrows them down
1078	by placing stall samples and execution counts beside individual SASS instructions. The Source page
1079	then reveals where those waits are concentrated. If the binary contains line information and NCU can
1080	find the source file, the instructions are also correlated with CUDA source lines. The data comes from
1081	periodic sampling of warp stall reasons together with instruction counts and selected memory-access
1082	metrics.
1083	
1084	Because the `nvjet` GEMM is a library implementation, this tutorial does not have access to its CUDA
1085	source. The SASS view is still available. Reuse the earlier filter and collection conditions:
1086	
1087	```bash
1088	ncu \
1089	  --config-file off \
1090	  --profile-from-start off \
1091	  --kernel-name 'regex:.*nvjet_sm100.*' \
1092	  --launch-count 1 \
1093	  --section SourceCounters \
1094	  --replay-mode kernel \
1095	  --cache-control all \
1096	  --clock-control boost \
1097	  --pipeline-boost-state stable \
1098	  --export reports/bf16-gemm-source \
1099	  --force-overwrite \
1100	  python appendix/nsys_example.py \
1101	    --size 4096 \
1102	    --warmup-calls 500 \
1103	    --profile-once
1104	```
1105	
1106	Select SASS on the GUI's Source page, or print the same view in the terminal:
1107	
1108	```bash
1109	ncu --import reports/bf16-gemm-source.ncu-rep \
1110	    --page source \
1111	    --print-source sass
1112	```
1113	
1114	Start with `Warp Stall Sampling (Not-issued Samples)` and `Instructions Executed`. The first counts
1115	sampling observations taken when the warp scheduler issued no instruction; the second counts
1116	executions of the corresponding SASS instruction per warp. If `WarpStateStats` was dominated by
1117	`Long Scoreboard` and the corresponding samples cluster around a particular load, that instruction
1118	becomes a candidate for closer inspection. These values come from periodic sampling and
1119	identify hotspot locations. Determining whether the data came from L1, L2, or DRAM still requires
1120	the kernel-wide evidence in `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis` together with the code's memory-access pattern.
1121	
1122	For a TIRx kernel that you compile yourself, the SASS can also be correlated with the generated CUDA
1123	source. First select NVCC, retain the generated source, and enable line information:
1124	
1125	```bash
1126	export TVM_CUDA_COMPILE_MODE=nvcc
1127	export TVM_KERNEL_DUMP="$PWD/reports/tvm-kernels"
1128	mkdir -p "$TVM_KERNEL_DUMP"
1129	```
1130	
1131	After setting the variables, rerun the workload in a fresh process so that the target kernel is
1132	recompiled with these settings. The following template collects the report; replace
1133	`YOUR_KERNEL_NAME` and the program path on the final line:
1134	
1135	```bash
1136	ncu \
1137	  --config-file off \
1138	  --kernel-name 'regex:.*YOUR_KERNEL_NAME.*' \
1139	  --launch-count 1 \
1140	  --section SourceCounters \
1141	  --replay-mode kernel \
1142	  --cache-control all \
1143	  --clock-control boost \
1144	  --pipeline-boost-state stable \
1145	  --import-source yes \
1146	  --source-folders "$TVM_KERNEL_DUMP" \
1147	  --export reports/tirx-source \
1148	  --force-overwrite \
1149	  python path/to/your_workload.py
1150	```
1151	
1152	Open `ncu-ui reports/tirx-source.ncu-rep` and use the CUDA/SASS correlation on the Source page. The
1153	terminal equivalent is
1154	`ncu --import reports/tirx-source.ncu-rep --page source --print-source cuda,sass`.
1155	If `executable` is your TIRx compilation result,
1156	`executable.mod.imports[0].inspect_source("cuda")` prints the generated source for manual inspection.
1157	NCU's line-by-line correlation depends on line information embedded in the binary during this
1158	recompilation.
1159	
1160	#### Test the Hypothesis with a Code Change
1161	
1162	Because this example calls the library-provided `torch.mm`, we cannot modify the kernel implementation
1163	here. The following steps give concrete modifications and validation checks for a custom TIRx kernel
1164	or another DSL kernel.
1165	
1166	To test the hypothesis that the kernel has too few resident warps to hide L1TEX latency, adjust the
1167	tile, block, or pipeline stages to reduce `Registers Per Thread` and
1168	`Dynamic Shared Memory Per Block`. Then recheck both block limits. A second block can reside only
1169	if both `Block Limit Registers` and `Block Limit Shared Mem` rise from one to at least two; improving
1170	only one is insufficient. Reducing register use can cause spills into local memory, and reducing
1171	shared-memory use may reduce data reuse. Also confirm that every other block limit is at least two,
1172	then inspect NCU's recalculated theoretical active blocks and occupancy. Use the latency measurement
1173	to determine whether the trade-off helps overall.
1174	
1175	For a separate experiment, hold residency constant while moving a load or prefetch earlier or
1176	shortening the dependency chain. If `Long Scoreboard` and latency fall together, that supports the
1177	explanation that warps now spend less time waiting for data. Because this metric is normalized per
1178	issued instruction, a decrease in this value alone does not establish a speedup. Change one key
1179	factor at a time, then check three things:
1180	
1181	1. **Correctness:** Compare both outputs with the same reference on the same inputs and with the same
1182	   tolerance. The current script already performs an FP32 reference check before timing or collection
1183	   begins; use the same reference and tolerance after substituting your own implementation.
1184	2. **Predicted metrics:** Collect the same NCU sections again and inspect the metrics relevant to the
1185	   prediction: for a residency experiment, inspect theoretical/active and eligible/issued warps;
1186	   for a dependency-chain experiment, inspect `Long Scoreboard`. Higher occupancy shows that the
1187	   residency experiment reached its resource target; the next check determines whether that change
1188	   also improves latency.
1189	3. **Actual latency:** Disable Proton, Nsight Systems, and NCU. Measure both implementations with
1190	   exactly the same shape, dtype, input policy, warm-up, CUDA event boundary, and sample count used
1191	   at the beginning.
1192	
1193	```bash
1194	python appendix/nsys_example.py \
1195	  --size 4096 \
1196	  --warmup-calls 500 \
1197	  --event-samples 20
1198	```
1199	
1200	Compare the unprofiled medians before and after the change, and inspect sample variation as well. If
1201	the correctness check passes, the metrics change as predicted, and CUDA event time decreases
1202	consistently, the hypothesis is supported. If the NCU metrics move as expected but latency does not
1203	improve, check whether another bottleneck has emerged or the original hypothesis was incomplete.
1204	
1205	## Use IKET to Inspect Phases Inside a DSL Kernel
1206	
1207	IKET (In-Kernel Event Tracing) adds an internal timeline to a warp-specialized TIRx kernel. Nsight
1208	Systems shows the beginning and end of the whole kernel, NCU aggregates hardware metrics across the
1209	launch, and IKET records when each warp role is active in marked regions such as producer, wait, and
1210	consumer.
1211	
1212	### Run a Complete Example
1213	
1214	TVM 0.26 uses the `cutlass-4.6.0` IKET profile, which pins the profiling dependencies to specific
1215	versions. For the CUDA 13 environment used in this chapter, install the matching dependencies and
1216	confirm that `run-iket` is available:
1217	
1218	```bash
1219	python -m pip install \
1220	  'nvidia-cutlass-dsl[cu13]==4.6.0' \
1221	  'nvidia-cuda-nvdisasm==13.3.73' \
1222	  'nvidia-cuda-nvrtc==13.2.78'
1223	run-iket --help
1224	```
1225	
1226	The complete script below is available as `appendix/iket_example.py`. One CTA contains two warps.
1227	Warp 0 moves 256 elements from global to shared memory, both warps meet at a CTA barrier, and warp 1
1228	reads shared memory, computes the result, and writes it out. Three `range_push()` / `range_pop()`
1229	pairs mark the producer, wait, and consumer regions:
1230	
1231	```python
1232	"""Minimal TIRx workload with IKET ranges for two warp roles."""
1233	
1234	from pathlib import Path
1235	
1236	import numpy as np
1237	
1238	import tvm
1239	from tvm.script import tirx as T
1240	from tvm.tirx.cuda import iket
1241	
1242	
1243	N = 256
1244	ELEMS_PER_LANE = 8
1245	
1246	
1247	@T.prim_func
1248	def warp_role_example(inp: T.Buffer((N,), "float32"), out: T.Buffer((N,), "float32")):
1249	    T.device_entry()
1250	    profiler = iket.IketProfiler()
1251	    warp_id = T.warp_id([2])
1252	    lane = T.lane_id([32])
1253	    shared = T.alloc_buffer((N,), "float32", scope="shared")
1254	
1255	    profiler.mark("kernel_start", warp_id)
1256	    if warp_id == 0:
1257	        profiler.range_push("producer_load")
1258	        for i in T.serial(ELEMS_PER_LANE, unroll=False):
1259	            index = i * 32 + lane
1260	            shared[index] = inp[index]
1261	        profiler.range_pop()
1262	
1263	    profiler.range_push("wait_for_data")
1264	    T.cuda.cta_sync()
1265	    profiler.range_pop()
1266	
1267	    if warp_id == 1:
1268	        profiler.range_push("consumer_compute")
1269	        for i in T.serial(ELEMS_PER_LANE, unroll=False):
1270	            index = i * 32 + lane
1271	            out[index] = shared[index] * T.float32(2) + T.float32(1)
1272	        profiler.range_pop()
1273	
1274	
1275	def profile_workload():
1276	    target = tvm.target.Target({"kind": "cuda", "arch": "sm_100a"})
1277	    executable = tvm.compile(warp_role_example, target=target, tir_pipeline="tirx")
1278	    module = executable.jit()
1279	
1280	    input_numpy = np.arange(N, dtype=np.float32)
1281	    inp = tvm.runtime.tensor(input_numpy, device=tvm.cuda())
1282	    out = tvm.runtime.empty((N,), "float32", device=tvm.cuda())
1283	    module.main(inp, out)
1284	    tvm.cuda().sync()
1285	
1286	    expected = input_numpy * 2 + 1
1287	    np.testing.assert_array_equal(out.numpy(), expected)
1288	
1289	
1290	def main():
1291	    result = iket.run(
1292	        profile_workload,
1293	        output_dir=Path("reports/iket-warp-roles"),
1294	        postprocess="all",
1295	        clobber=True,
1296	        timeout=600.0,
1297	    )
1298	    print(f"IKET output directory: {result.output_dir}")
1299	    for path in (*result.json_traces, *result.perfetto_traces, *result.html_reports):
1300	        print(f"IKET artifact: {path}")
1301	
1302	
1303	if __name__ == "__main__":
1304	    main()
1305	```
1306	
1307	Run it directly on a B200:
1308	
1309	```bash
1310	python appendix/iket_example.py
1311	```
1312	
1313	`iket.run` restarts the current script inside the IKET collection process and calls
1314	`profile_workload()`. Keeping `tvm.compile()` and `.jit()` inside that function ensures that the
1315	kernel is compiled and loaded while IKET recording is active. The script also verifies that the
1316	output equals `input * 2 + 1`.
1317	
1318	With `postprocess="all"`, `iket.run` writes JSON, `*.pftrace`, and HTML artifacts to
1319	`reports/iket-warp-roles`. Load the `*.pftrace` file in Perfetto to inspect `producer_load`,
1320	`wait_for_data`, and `consumer_compute`. Warp 1 usually reaches the barrier before warp 0, giving it
1321	a longer `wait_for_data` region. For an H100, change `sm_100a` in the script to `sm_90a`.
1322	
1323	### Add IKET Annotations to Your Own Kernel
1324	
1325	Create an `IketProfiler` inside the `PrimFunc`. Use `mark()` for an instantaneous event, and use
1326	matched `range_push()` / `range_pop()` or `range_start()` / `range_end()` calls around a phase. Keep
1327	IKET ranges balanced along every control-flow path that a warp may take. Mark waiting explicitly, as
1328	the example does with `wait_for_data`.
1329	
1330	Keep compilation and the first JIT load inside the function passed to `iket.run`. IKET supports
1331	Hopper and newer architectures and validates the CUTLASS DSL packages, NVRTC, `nvdisasm`, and related
1332	binaries against the pinned profile. The recording code inserted by IKET changes the generated
1333	kernel and adds overhead, so use the IKET trace to study phases and warp roles. For reported latency,
1334	use the uninstrumented CUDA event benchmark. See
1335	[`python/tvm/backend/cuda/iket.py`](https://github.com/apache/tvm/blob/v0.26.0/python/tvm/backend/cuda/iket.py)
1336	and the
1337	[NVIDIA IKET guide](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/v4.6.0/media/docs/pythonDSL/cute_dsl_general/iket_profiling.rst)
1338	for the complete API and trace options.
1339
